# R3 Digest — Provan, *1 and 2 Kings* (NIBC), §§19–25

**Source:** Iain W. Provan, *1 and 2 Kings*, NIBC (1995)  
**Slice:** `R3_division_1529-1942.txt` (raw lines 1529–1942)  
**Scope:** Kingdom torn (1 Kgs 12:1–24); Jeroboam’s sin/calves (12:25–33); man of God from Judah (13:1–34); ends of Jeroboam & Rehoboam (14:1–31); Abijam/Asa (15:1–24); Nadab to Ahab / Omride rise (15:25–16:34)  
**Attribution:** All interpretive claims below are Provan’s (or Provan reporting the authors of Kings); wiki voice not used.  
**Established targets:** [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[solomon]], [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]  
**NEW flags:** sustained figure treatment of **Jeroboam**, **Rehoboam**, **Asa**, **Ahab** (and related **Ahijah**, man of God / Bethel prophet, **Baasha**, **Omri**, **Jezebel** as narrative supports)

---

### C-R3-01 — Schism as second Exodus: Jeroboam/Moses, Rehoboam/Pharaoh
**Claim:** Provan frames the tearing of the kingdom (ch. 11 threat now realized) as a second exodus: Jeroboam leads Israel from “slavery” under the house of David as Moses led Israel from Pharaoh; Rehoboam’s hard heart, like Pharaoh’s, precipitates the schism under God’s will.  
**Quote:** “As Moses led his people out from slavery under the house of the Egyptian Pharaoh, so Jeroboam will lead Israel out from ‘slavery’ under the house of David; as God hardened Pharaoh’s heart in order to accomplish all his will, so the hardness of Rehoboam’s heart will precipitate this schism also.”  
**Locus:** §19 intro (slice ~ll. 11); 1 Kgs 12:1–24  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[solomon]], [[david]]; NEW Jeroboam, Rehoboam

---

### C-R3-02 — Jeroboam-as-Moses becomes Jeroboam-as-Aaron; path to exile
**Claim:** The new exodus will be derailed when Jeroboam-as-Moses becomes Jeroboam-as-Aaron fashioning golden calves; eventual result is ejection and exile.  
**Quote:** “The exodus will take Israel towards a new promised land, but they will soon be led off their path, as ‘Jeroboam as Moses’ is transformed into ‘Jeroboam as Aaron,’ who fashions golden calves for them to worship. Eventually the result will be ejection from their land and exile in another.”  
**Locus:** §19 intro (slice ~ll. 11)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-03 — Shechem as covenant / Joseph / anti-kingship site
**Claim:** Rehoboam’s coronation venue Shechem is chosen (Provan argues) for its pre-monarchic resonances: covenant renewal (Josh 24), Joseph’s bones closing the exodus story, and Abimelech’s brief wicked kingship (Judg 8–9)—ideal for testing whether kingship will fit the covenant people of God.  
**Quote:** “It is a place of covenant renewal (Josh. 24:1–27)… the place where Joseph’s bones are buried… also the place where kingship first, if briefly, intruded itself into the tribal life of Israel… Shechem is an ideal place, therefore, to which a prospective king might be invited if you wished to ask him… how his kingship was going to be exercised so as to be consonant with the nature of the covenant people of God.”  
**Locus:** §19 on 12:1–4 (slice ~ll. 15)  
**Targets:** [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Rehoboam

---

### C-R3-04 — People’s complaint: identity under Solomon = Egypt’s harsh labor
**Claim:** Under Solomon the people’s identity is “confused”: no longer free in the land but again under harsh labor / heavy yoke as in Egypt (Exod 1:14; 2:23); Jeroboam appears as a second Moses, with MT reluctance paralleling Exod 4.  
**Quote:** “They are no longer the people set free to live in the promised land. They have become once more a people under harsh labor, as they were in Egypt… Jeroboam appears as a kind of second Moses… The similarity even extends in the MT… to a certain reluctance to take on such a role (cf. Exod. 4:1–17).”  
**Locus:** §19 on 12:1–4 (slice ~ll. 17)  
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-05 — Authors withhold verdict on Solomon’s “heavy yoke”
**Claim:** Provan notes the authors do not commit on whether Solomon’s regime was unduly harsh; they distinguish Canaanite *mas* from Israelite *sēḇel*, and chs. 3–8 do not sound oppressive—though 9:10–10:29 may prepare for this speech.  
**Quote:** “It is the claim of ‘all Israel’ that Solomon’s regime… has been unduly harsh. The authors do not commit themselves on the point. They do want us to think differently about the mas… and the sēḇel… There are perhaps hints in 9:10–10:29, however, that they are preparing us for Israel’s speech here.”  
**Locus:** §19 add. n. 12:4 (slice ~ll. 47)  
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

---

### C-R3-06 — Rehoboam as Pharaoh: foolish counsel, divine hardening
**Claim:** Elders advise servant-leadership from below (12:7); Rehoboam takes the hard line of his peers (whips → scorpions), replaying Pharaoh’s increase of oppression (Exod 5); he *must* so act because the LORD has ordained Ahijah’s word (v. 15)—“this turn of events was from the LORD,” like Pharaoh’s hard heart.  
**Quote:** “When he does so… he is behaving exactly as Pharaoh had behaved before him… He is bound to act thus, however, for the LORD has ordained that his word to Jeroboam through Ahijah should come to pass (v. 15)… ‘Nor did this king… listen to the people, for this turn of events was from the LORD.’”  
**Locus:** §19 on 12:5–15 (slice ~ll. 19)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]]; NEW Rehoboam, Ahijah; [[deuteronomistic-history]]

---

### C-R3-07 — Play on ʿḇḏ “serve”: king must serve to keep servants
**Claim:** Hebrew root ʿḇḏ runs through 12:1–15: Israelites as servants are acceptable in principle, but if the king wants them as servants he must be a servant to them and demand less.  
**Quote:** “There is a play on the Hb. root ʿḇḏ, ‘to serve,’ throughout 12:1–15… The king has the Israelites as servants, to which they do not in principle object; but if he really wants them as servants, he must be a servant to them and demand less service.”  
**Locus:** §19 add. n. 12:7 (slice ~ll. 49)  
**Targets:** [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-2-kings]]

---

### C-R3-08 — “All Israel” and legitimacy: corporate decree vs de facto Judah
**Claim:** Against the common view that “all Israel” in 12:20 means only northern tribes, Provan argues the phrase still evokes the united-kingdom entity of 11:42 / 12:1: politically/theoretically Jeroboam is legitimate ruler of the whole; Rehoboam retains de facto control of Judah—paralleling the theology of 11:11–13 (tear, yet not the whole).  
**Quote:** “Politically and theoretically speaking, Jeroboam is the legitimate ruler of the whole kingdom and Rehoboam has no legitimacy at all… Nevertheless, in his sovereign grace God has decreed that Rehoboam should hold Judah and that Jeroboam should have ten tribes rather than twelve… Political theory and political reality are not permitted to match up.”  
**Locus:** §19 on 12:16–20 (slice ~ll. 21); add. n. 12:20 (slice ~ll. 55)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[david]]; NEW Jeroboam, Rehoboam

---

### C-R3-09 — Shemaiah prevents war; God as third party between brothers
**Claim:** Rehoboam’s military bid is stopped by Shemaiah’s oracle that the schism is of God; continuous N–S war will follow (14:30; 15:6, 16) because neither side fully accepts God’s decision—God is “firmly on his own side, a third party”; peace comes only when they see they are brothers (v. 24; cf. 1 Kgs 22:44).  
**Quote:** “In this case, he is firmly on his own side, a third party in a conflict between two factions who cannot accept his decision. All the wars will therefore come to nothing, until the two sides come to see that they are indeed brothers (v. 24; cf. 1 Kgs. 22, esp. v. 44).”  
**Locus:** §19 on 12:21–24 (slice ~ll. 23)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]]; NEW Rehoboam, Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-10 — Adoram/Adoniram: Rehoboam-as-Pharaoh imposing *mas*
**Claim:** Sending Adoram (forced labor) is not re-imposing existing *mas* on Israel (Israel had not been under it per 9:15–23) but treating Israel as if still in Egypt / as Canaanites—first harsh move of the new regime.  
**Quote:** “Rehoboam is intent, as ‘Pharaoh,’ on regarding Israel as if they were still in Egypt, putting them now under conditions of forced labor… The Israelites are to be treated under the new regime as if they were Canaanites.”  
**Locus:** §19 add. n. 12:18 (slice ~ll. 53)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]]; NEW Rehoboam

---

### C-R3-11 — Jeroboam’s characteristic sin: golden calves → exile refrain
**Claim:** Jeroboam’s facilitation of golden-calf worship is the northern kingdom’s characteristic sin constantly referred to thereafter (e.g. 15:26, 34) and leading eventually to exile (2 Kgs 17:20–23).  
**Quote:** “It is Jeroboam’s action in facilitating such worship that will constantly be referred to in the narrative about the northern kingdom that follows (e.g., 15:26, 34) as Israel’s characteristic sin that leads eventually to exile in a foreign land (2 Kgs. 17:20–23).”  
**Locus:** §20 intro (slice ~ll. 75)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-12 — Root of Jeroboam’s sin: inability to trust God / religion as political control
**Claim:** Jeroboam’s downfall is inability to trust—people, his own legitimacy (still calling Rehoboam “their lord”), and above all God despite Ahijah’s word (11:31–39). He fears the Jerusalem temple more than his own obedience (11:38); religion becomes “simply an aspect of political control,” producing Dan and Bethel as rival centers.  
**Quote:** “Most of all, he does not trust God… He fears that the presence of the temple of the LORD in Jerusalem (12:27) will be a more decisive factor… than his own obedience (11:38)… In his thinking, religion becomes simply an aspect of political control.”  
**Locus:** §20 on 12:25–30 (slice ~ll. 77–79)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]]; NEW Jeroboam; Ahijah

---

### C-R3-13 — Golden calves: Jeroboam/Aaron; Exodus 32:4 echo; living God vs image
**Claim:** Construction of two golden calves transforms Jeroboam/Moses into Jeroboam/Aaron (Exod 32); 1 Kgs 12:28 (“Here are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt”) is almost exactly Exod 32:4. Following Solomon into sin brings judgment: God is living Lord of history, not a convenient symbol; cannot be captured in an image any more than confined in a temple.  
**Quote:** “Jeroboam/Moses is transformed into Jeroboam/Aaron (Exod. 32:1–35)… His words to them in 1 Kings 12:28… are, indeed, almost exactly the words with which the people greet the construction of the first calf (Exod. 32:4)… God cannot be captured in an image any more than be confined in a temple.”  
**Locus:** §20 on 12:25–30 (slice ~ll. 81)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-14 — Bethel “house of high places”: rival temple, priesthood, eighth-month feast
**Claim:** NIV obscures *bêṯ bāmôṯ* (v. 31) as mere “shrines”; Provan reads a singular illegitimate “house of high places” competing with the Jerusalem “house of the LORD,” with non-Levite priests and a Tabernacles-like festival in the eighth month of Jeroboam’s choosing—evoking Aaron’s altar and self-chosen festival (Exod 32:5) and Solomon’s temple dedication.  
**Quote:** “Rehoboam has a ‘house’ in Jerusalem; Jeroboam needs a ‘house’ to compete with it. So he builds a ‘house of high places’ (i.e., an illegitimate temple in the singular)… an illegitimate festival, which takes place in the eighth month—a month of his own choosing… We assume that this is Jeroboam’s version of the Feast of Tabernacles… The story is still evoking memories of Aaron.”  
**Locus:** §20 on 12:31–33 (slice ~ll. 83–85)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-15 — Triple illegitimacy: Deut 12 temple site; blurred priesthood; invented date
**Claim:** Jeroboam’s system infringes Deut 12 (temple outside Jerusalem), blurs set-apart Levites vs people (cf. Num 3–4), and invents a festival with “no divine significance”; question posed: if Solomon’s apostasy lost the kingdom, what will Jeroboam’s quicker departure cost him?  
**Quote:** “The new king has built a temple outside Jerusalem that infringes the prohibition in Deuteronomy 12; created a priesthood that has blurred the important distinction between those set apart by God for priestly service… and invented a festival celebrated on a date with no divine significance whatsoever… if Solomon’s eventual apostasy lost him the kingdom, what will Jeroboam’s much quicker departure from the LORD’s commandments cost him?”  
**Locus:** §20 on 12:31–33 (slice ~ll. 85–87)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[solomon]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-16 — Against “misunderstood Yahwist” reading of the calves
**Claim:** Provan rejects the common scholarly claim that Jeroboam only substituted calves for ark/cherubim as Yahwistic worship and was “misrepresented”: from Deut 4:15–24 / 1 Kgs 14:9 viewpoint, representation-worship *is* idolatry (“other gods”); 14:15 already associates calves with Canaanite worship; sincerity is not enough.  
**Quote:** “You cannot worship the LORD using representations of him, for then you are not worshiping him at all but ‘other gods’ (1 Kgs. 14:9). Whatever Jeroboam thinks he is doing with his calves, it is idolatry from the point of view of these passages… Sincerity—if that is what it is—is not enough.”  
**Locus:** §20 add. n. 12:28 (slice ~ll. 109)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[iain-provan]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-17 — Bethel as royal sanctuary: religion vs free prophecy (Amos parallel)
**Claim:** Bethel is the more important sanctuary for the authors; Amos 7:10–17 again shows religion as political control vs God’s free prophetic word—as Jeroboam will shortly discover.  
**Quote:** “Bethel also appears in the book of Amos… as the royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom… Amaziah suggests that Amos has no right to preach against the king at Bethel… Amos’ response is to assert God’s freedom to speak wherever and however God chooses. The true prophet is beyond human control—as Jeroboam son of Nebat will shortly discover for himself.”  
**Locus:** §20 add. n. 12:29 (slice ~ll. 111)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-18 — Man of God: Jeroboam’s temple dedication cut off; dynasty already assumed doomed
**Claim:** Jeroboam at the altar like Solomon (8:22) never gets to dedicate: a man of God from Judah threatens the altar (13:2–3) looking toward Josiah (2 Kgs 23:15–20), already assuming the end of northern dynasties; short-term sign (split altar, poured ashes) authenticates long-term prophecy; king’s hand withered then healed shows he has no power over prophet or God.  
**Quote:** “as Solomon’s temple was built in fulfillment of a prophetic promise about both temple and dynasty (2 Sam. 7:1–17), the building of Jeroboam’s temple evokes prophetic threats… which in due course will come to fulfillment in the destruction of both dynasty and temple… his words already assume the end of the dynasty (even before it has begun).”  
**Locus:** §21 intro + 13:1–6 (slice ~ll. 135–137)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[solomon]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-19 — Prophetic hospitality ban: freedom from mortal obligation
**Claim:** Man of God must not eat/drink or return by the same way (13:9); Provan reads this (and invitations by king and old prophet) against true prophets free of mortal obligation (Amos 7) vs false prophets who speak what people wish (Mic 3; 1 Kgs 22)—attempts to “buy” reversal of curse on altar/tomb.  
**Quote:** “We may be intended to read Jeroboam’s invitation to dine and receive a gift (v. 7), then, as an attempt to buy the Judean’s loyalty. If the prophet can reverse God’s judgment in the small matter of the hand, perhaps he can also exchange the curse on the altar for a blessing.”  
**Locus:** §21 on 13:7–30 (slice ~ll. 139)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Jeroboam

---

### C-R3-20 — Even prophets under the word: false prophet, true word, lion judgment
**Claim:** The Judean is led astray by a false claim of another prophecy; true word condemns him for defying the LORD’s command; lion kills him (miraculous restraint of beast/donkey in 13:28); God’s law stands over everyone—even prophets—and God can use false prophets occasionally to speak truth.  
**Quote:** “The point is thus forcefully made that he ought to have followed through the word of the LORD that he had received… rather than being led off his path by another’s prophetic claim… It is further made clear that God’s law stands over everyone—that even prophets must obey it, or face judgment—and that God can use even false prophets occasionally to speak the truth.”  
**Locus:** §21 on 13:7–30 (slice ~ll. 141); add. n. 13:28 (slice ~ll. 165)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

---

### C-R3-21 — Old prophet’s bones: self-preservation for 2 Kgs 23, not piety
**Claim:** Request to lay bones beside the Judean’s is not benevolent desire to be remembered but a plan to avoid desecration predicted in 13:2/32—a plan that works in 2 Kgs 23:17–18.  
**Quote:** “it is much more likely that his concern is not so much to be remembered in the grave as to be allowed to remain in the grave… this is his alternative plan (after his hospitality stratagem failed) to avoid the desecration of his bones… As it turns out, this second plan is one that works (2 Kgs. 23:17–18).”  
**Locus:** §21 add. n. 13:31 (slice ~ll. 167)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]]

---

### C-R3-22 — Jeroboam hardens: šwḇ wordplay; sin that puts everlasting dynasty out of reach
**Claim:** Despite ch. 13’s warnings, Jeroboam does not repent (unlike Ahab in 21:28–29) but proliferates the cult; play on *šwḇ* “return” links man of God’s fatal retracing of steps with Jeroboam’s retracing—persistence in idolatry is “the sin” that dooms the house and forfeits the everlasting dynasty of 11:38.  
**Quote:** “And because all the warnings of chapter 13 have led him, not to repentance (like Ahab in 1 Kgs. 21:28–29), but to a hardening of heart, the destruction of his house is now assured (v. 34). This was the sin—this persistence in idolatry—that led him to disaster. His adherence to his religious reforms has put the prize of an everlasting dynasty out of reach.”  
**Locus:** §21 on 13:31–34 (slice ~ll. 143); add. n. 13:33 (slice ~ll. 171)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[davidic-covenant]]; NEW Jeroboam, Ahab

---

### C-R3-23 — Ahijah oracle: Jeroboam failed to be like David; rʿʿ / rāʿâ; ḵrṯ vs Davidic “never fail”
**Claim:** Disguised wife cannot manipulate the blind prophet who “sees” via God; Jeroboam failed to be like David (14:8; 11:38), worshiped other gods like Solomon; because he did *rʿʿ* (evil), God brings *rāʿâ* (disaster)—every male *ḵrṯ* “cut off,” bodies for dogs/birds—stark contrast to Davidic *lōʾ ḵrṯ* “never fail” (2:4; 8:25; 9:5) and why God is harsher with Jeroboam than with Solomon/Rehoboam.  
**Quote:** “Jeroboam has failed to be like David (14:8; cf. 11:38); he has, like Solomon, worshiped other gods (v. 9). Because he has done… evil (Hb. rʿʿ)… God is going to bring disaster (rāʿâ) on the house of Jeroboam… David will always have a descendant… but Jeroboam will be harshly deprived of descendants (Hb. ḵrṯ, cut off). This is, of course, why God deals so much more leniently with Solomon (and Rehoboam…) than he does with Jeroboam.”  
**Locus:** §22 on 14:1–11 (slice ~ll. 193–195)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Jeroboam, Rehoboam; Ahijah

### C-R3-24 — Abijah’s death as relative blessing; David’s house not subverted by sin
**Claim:** The boy’s death is tragedy but burial-blessing vs unburied house; echoes David’s lost child (2 Sam 12) yet without destruction of dynasty—Solomon follows Bathsheba’s first son; “Sin cannot subvert David’s promise, as it can and does Jeroboam’s”; David’s relative righteousness (even with Uriah exception, 15:5) is not the entire explanation for the distinction.  
**Quote:** “Sin cannot subvert David’s promise, as it can and does Jeroboam’s. We are reminded of this in a context where David’s righteousness is once again stressed (v. 8); for David certainly did not do only what was right in God’s eyes in the matter of Uriah the Hittite (cf. 1 Kgs. 15:5). Not for the first time in 1 Kings we are being invited to ponder on the real reason why a distinction has been made between David and other kings.”  
**Locus:** §22 on 14:12–13 (slice ~ll. 197–199)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Jeroboam

### C-R3-25 — Northern kingdom as reed; exile beyond the Euphrates (Assyria); Asherah linked to calves
**Claim:** Ahijah looks beyond the house to Israel’s instability (“reed swaying in the water”) and exile beyond the Euphrates (=Assyria, 2 Kgs 17); Jeroboam’s disobedience affects whole kingdom destiny. Asherah poles (14:15) already associate golden calves with foreign-deity worship that will break out under Ahab.  
**Quote:** “In the absence of a strong dynasty… they are destined to know only the instability of a reed swaying in the water… and eventual exile in a land beyond the River Euphrates… the land beyond the river, it turns out, is Assyria… The golden calves are thus already being associated with the worship of foreign deities that will break out in Israel with a vengeance during the reign of Ahab (1 Kgs. 16:29ff.).”  
**Locus:** §22 on 14:14–16 (slice ~ll. 201); add. n. 14:15 (slice ~ll. 233)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]; NEW Jeroboam, Ahab

### C-R3-26 — Immediate fulfillment as sign; Nadab succession temporary
**Claim:** Boy’s death at Tirzah (like split altar) signs that the whole oracle will come to pass; Nadab’s succession is only temporary because the house is doomed as David’s is secure.  
**Quote:** “Like the splitting of the altar in 13:5, the fulfillment of this immediate prophecy functions as a sign that everything else will also come to pass. We cannot regard the succession of Nadab, then, as anything other than temporary; for we know that Jeroboam’s house is doomed, just as surely as we know that David’s is secure.”  
**Locus:** §22 on 14:17–20 (slice ~ll. 203)  
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Jeroboam

### C-R3-27 — Royal disguise theme: God, not king, determines events
**Claim:** Disguise motif (also 1 Sam 28; 2 Chron 35; later 1 Kgs 20; 22) underlines that God, not the king, determines the course of events.  
**Quote:** “The theme of royal disguise appears in other places in the OT where the point is made that, whatever the king may think, it is God and not the king who determines the course of events.”  
**Locus:** §22 add. n. 14:2 (slice ~ll. 225)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R3-28 — Judean formula unusual: *Judah* did evil; Ammonite mother; same fate hinted
**Claim:** Rehoboam’s formula is unusual: not that Rehoboam but that *Judah* did evil (v. 22)—nation-wide high places and pre-conquest practices; mother’s Ammonite identity (11:1–6) twice noted; implicit threat that Judah too will be “driven out”; authors already hint north and south equally sinful and heading same way (language mirrored in 2 Kgs 17:7–17 / 14:22–24).  
**Quote:** “here we are told (v. 22), not that Rehoboam did evil in the eyes of the LORD, but that Judah did so… Right at the beginning of their account of the divided kingdom… the authors are hinting to us that both north and south are equally sinful… and thus heading for the same fate.”  
**Locus:** §23 on 14:21–24 (slice ~ll. 259)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[solomon]]; NEW Rehoboam

### C-R3-29 — No end-oracle for David’s house: Shishak as 2 Sam 7:14 discipline; lamp vs Abijah’s death
**Claim:** No prophetic end-oracle for David’s house matching 14:7–16; Shishak’s raid replaces golden age with “bronze,” peace with war—little more than fatherly discipline of 2 Sam 7:14. Juxtaposition of Ammonite mother with chosen Jerusalem (v. 21) points to God’s choice of David/Jerusalem as *the* explanation for different treatment; symbolized by Jeroboam’s good-ish son dying vs Rehoboam’s bad Abijam succeeding.  
**Quote:** “All this, however, is little more than the fatherly discipline of 2 Samuel 7:14… it is, of course, God’s choice of David and Jerusalem… that is the only explanation for the difference in the treatment of David and Jeroboam. And what symbolizes this difference more than anything is that Jeroboam’s son Abijah dies, even though there is some good in him (14:13), whereas Rehoboam’s son Abijam… lives to succeed him, even though he is just as bad as his father.”  
**Locus:** §23 on 14:25–31 (slice ~ll. 261–263)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Rehoboam, Jeroboam, Asa (setup)

### C-R3-30 — Treasure-loss notices hyperbolic series to 2 Kgs 25
**Claim:** Shishak’s “took everything” is first of a hyperbolic *kōl* series of temple/palace treasure losses culminating in 2 Kgs 25—not to be taken literally.  
**Quote:** “This the first of a series of notices in Kings about the loss of treasure from the temple and the palace… the culmination of which will come in 2 Kgs. 25. The everything… is not to be taken literally. Hebrew kōl… is often used hyperbolically.”  
**Locus:** §23 add. n. 14:26 (slice ~ll. 285)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]]

### C-R3-31 — Abijam/Asa set the Judean pattern: like David or not
**Claim:** Abijam is the characteristically bad Judean king (idolatry of late Solomon/Rehoboam); Asa the characteristically good (relatively faithful like David and early Solomon); together they set the pattern by which all subsequent Judean kings are measured as “like David” or not.  
**Quote:** “Abijam is the characteristically bad Judean king… Asa is the characteristically good Judean king… These two between them set the pattern for all subsequent Judean kings, who are measured in terms of whether they have been ‘like David’ or not.”  
**Locus:** §24 intro (slice ~ll. 305)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]]; NEW Asa, Rehoboam (line)

### C-R3-32 — Lamp for David’s sake; piety inadequate as full explanation
**Claim:** Despite Abijam’s undevoted heart, “for David’s sake” God gives a lamp in Jerusalem (15:4; 11:36)—dynasty secure, sin cannot ultimately affect it; authors again offer David’s “right” deeds as reason yet note Uriah sin and grace—piety is model but “cannot be the complete explanation for the favor shown by God to the Davidic line.”  
**Quote:** “For David’s sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem (v. 4; cf. 11:36). This dynasty, unlike Jeroboam’s, is secure; sin cannot affect its fortunes in any ultimate sense… David’s piety is indeed a model for other kings; but it cannot be the complete explanation for the favor shown by God to the Davidic line.”  
**Locus:** §24 on 15:1–8 (slice ~ll. 309)  
**Targets:** [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[1-2-kings]]

---

### C-R3-33 — Asa’s reform: full commitment with high-place limit; points to Hezekiah/Josiah
**Claim:** Asa did right; heart fully committed all his life (not perfection but Davidic pattern without idolatry): expels shrine prostitutes, removes idols, deposes Maacah’s Asherah object; did *not* remove high places (like early Solomon 3:2–3) yet dedicated treasures—points forward to Hezekiah (swr high places, 2 Kgs 18:4) and Josiah (Kidron burnings).  
**Quote:** “He did not remove (Hb. swr) the high places and focus his reformed worship only on the temple in Jerusalem, but otherwise he was exemplary… He is a good king—but he is not the best king Judah will have.”  
**Locus:** §24 on 15:9–15 (slice ~ll. 311); add. n. 15:12 wordplay (slice ~ll. 339)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[david]], [[solomon]]; NEW Asa

### C-R3-34 — Asa vs Baasha: faithfulness without Solomon’s glory; bribe to Aram; diseased feet
**Claim:** Asa’s long reign sees five northern kings before Ahab; war with Baasha and *šōḥaḏ* “bribe” to Ben-Hadad reverse Solomon’s empire-building (Asa suppliant, loses Israelite territory, imposes forced labor)—faithfulness like early Solomon no longer yields Solomon’s glory; times of humbling (11:39); diseased feet may hint late departure like Solomon (11:4).  
**Quote:** “Faithfulness like Solomon’s no longer brings Solomon’s glory in its wake. These are different times—times of humbling for David’s descendants (11:39)… Asa’s ultimate reward is diseased feet (15:23)—or is there just a hint here that Asa, too, departed from God in his old age (cf. 11:4) and was punished for doing so?”  
**Locus:** §24 on 15:16–24 (slice ~ll. 313–315)  
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[david]]; NEW Asa

### C-R3-35 — Maacah as mother/incest possibility; ʾēm not necessarily grandmother
**Claim:** Against NIV “grandmother,” Provan prefers reading *ʾēm* as mother in line with other Judean formulas, raising possibility Asa is product of incestuous Abijam–Maacah relationship—one evil among many.  
**Quote:** “We should consider the possibility, therefore, that the authors of Kings mean to say that Asa was the product of an incestuous relationship between Abijam and Maacah (cf. 15:2). It would be only one evil among the many that Abijam perpetrated.”  
**Locus:** §24 add. n. 15:10 (slice ~ll. 335)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Asa

### C-R3-36 — Ahijah fulfilled: Nadab short reign; Baasha destroys Jeroboam’s house
**Claim:** After Judean contrast is clear, prophecy against Jeroboam’s house is fulfilled: Nadab does evil two years; Baasha murders him and all Jeroboam’s family as Ahijah said (14:10–11); house of Issachar replaces house of Jeroboam.  
**Quote:** “Now, however, we shall hear that it all turned out as Ahijah had said… Baasha in turn kills all the other members of Jeroboam’s family, just as Ahijah had said he would (14:10–11). The house of Jeroboam is no more.”  
**Locus:** §25 intro + 15:25–32 (slice ~ll. 361–363)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Jeroboam; Ahijah, Baasha

### C-R3-37 — Baasha walks in Jeroboam’s sin; Jehu son of Hanani; dual causality
**Claim:** Baasha shows no understanding that God placed him on the throne; walks in Jeroboam’s ways/sin; Jehu announces same fate for his house; authors give almost equal narrative space to 24-year Baasha and 2-year Nadab because idolatry outweighs other achievements. Destroying Jeroboam’s house as ordained does not remove Baasha’s moral responsibility (predestination/free will mystery; cf. Hos 1:4 // 1 Kgs 21 / 2 Kgs 9–10).  
**Quote:** “The fact that the destruction of Jeroboam’s house was ordained by God did not mean that Baasha bore no moral responsibility for his actions… Both these texts raise in a very sharp way the mystery at the heart of God’s dealings with mortal beings.”  
**Locus:** §25 on 15:33–16:7 (slice ~ll. 365); add. n. 16:7 (slice ~ll. 399)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]]; NEW Jeroboam; Baasha

### C-R3-38 — Elah/Zimri/Omri: reed-in-water instability; Zimri seven days; Omri’s Samaria
**Claim:** Elah lasts two years, murdered by Zimri who butchers house and friends; Zimri fails after seven days as “all Israel” (tribal assembly, cf. 12:1ff.) elevates Omri; after struggle with Tibni, Omri rules. Only Omri event narrated: purchase of Samaria hill and new capital—life subsumed under “idolater”; extra-biblical Omri largely unimportant to authors. Samaria = city and by extension kingdom.  
**Quote:** “His life as king, too, is simply subsumed under the heading ‘idolater’ (vv. 25–26). He took the throne; he sinned; he died. Almost everything else (and extra-biblical evidence suggests there was quite a bit) is unimportant.”  
**Locus:** §25 on 16:8–28 (slice ~ll. 367–373); §21 add. n. 13:32 Samaria (slice ~ll. 169)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]]; NEW Ahab (setup Omride); Omri

### C-R3-39 — Ahab worst: Jeroboam’s sins + Jezebel + Baal temple in Samaria
**Claim:** Ahab is last and worst of kings rising in Asa’s Judean reign: walks in sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat *plus* marriage to Jezebel (cf. 3:1–3 foreign wives) leading to Baal worship (cf. Sidonian women/deity of 11:1, 5); now temple and altar for Baal in Samaria alongside Bethel calf cult—northern sins multiply.  
**Quote:** “the last is also the worst. He too walks in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, but he adds to this iniquity marriage to a foreign woman, Jezebel… who inevitably leads him into the worship of Baal… In addition to the temple and altar for the calf at Bethel there is now a temple and an altar for Baal in Samaria. The sins of the northern kingdom have multiplied.”  
**Locus:** §25 on 16:29–34 (slice ~ll. 375)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]]; NEW Ahab, Jeroboam; Jezebel

### C-R3-40 — Major theme of 1 Kgs 12–16: God’s control over history via prophetic word
**Claim:** Provan synthesizes chs. 12–16: major theme is God’s control over history—monarchs may think the LORD is not/should not be in politics, but God directs affairs so ultimate kingship is obvious; everything comes to pass as prophets say (David’s house stands; Jeroboam’s destroyed; Judah stable; Israel’s houses come and go); beyond even prophetic control (ch. 13); short- and long-term fulfillments.  
**Quote:** “As we look back over 1 Kings 12–16, it seems evident that their major theme is ‘God’s control over history.’ Monarchs may think that the LORD is not or should not be involved in politics, but the LORD is involved… Everything comes to pass just as the prophets say it will… Beyond human control—even prophetic control (1 Kgs. 13)—what God wills comes to pass.”  
**Locus:** §25 synthesis on 16:29–34 (slice ~ll. 377)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R3-41 — Omride delay and Elijah setup; Hiel/Jericho as long-horizon prophecy
**Claim:** Omri unlike Jeroboam/Baasha receives no fall-oracle; Ahab will reign ~20 years more—does this most sinful house confound the “reed” prophecy? No: judgment will be spoken/enacted though Omri’s house holds throne 100+ years; first channel is Elijah, “the most significant prophetic figure so far in northern Israel’s history,” confronting most sinful king Ahab. Close of 16:34 (Hiel rebuilds Jericho; Josh 6:26 as word of the LORD) reminds of long-term prophecy fulfillment; Bethelite Hiel signals contempt for prophecy and looming 13:2 / 2 Kgs 23 threat; Israel now embraces Canaanite religion rather than conquering Canaanites. God’s silences = patience; NT parallel on delayed but sure word.  
**Quote:** “Its first channel will be the most significant prophetic figure so far in northern Israel’s history. The most sinful of Israel’s kings, Ahab, will have to reckon with the most powerful of prophetic interventions, in the shape of Elijah… We should never confuse God’s long-term planning with an unwillingness or inability to communicate and to act in human history.”  
**Locus:** §25 synthesis + add. n. 16:34 (slice ~ll. 377, 403)  
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]; NEW Ahab; Omri, Elijah (setup)

**Claim:** Rehoboam’s “my little finger thicker than my father’s waist” may be sexual organ imagery (loins/potency), claiming to be a bigger man than Solomon—power boast of young men.  
**Quote:** “it may well be that the ‘little one’ is in fact the male sexual organ… Whatever is the case, the claim is that Rehoboam is a bigger man than his father—a power to be reckoned with.”  
**Locus:** §19 add. n. 12:10 (slice ~ll. 51)

**Claim:** Judah’s high-place cult includes sacred stones (possibly phallic; Deut 12:3), Asherah poles, and male (or mixed) shrine prostitutes (Hos 4:14; Deut 23:17–18)—abandoning first lover, making the LORD “jealous” (14:22).  
**Quote:** “Judah has abandoned its first lover for others and made him ‘jealous’ (v. 22).”

**Claim:** 15:6’s “war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam” under Abijam stresses continuity of the houses’ feud; Ben-Hadad/Aram who was adversary in Solomon’s apostasy (11:23–25) now opposes faithful Asa—“another sure sign that the times have changed.”  
**Quote:** “The adversary raised up there against Solomon in his apostasy now opposes Asa in his faithfulness—another sure sign that the times have changed.”

### C-R3-45 — Zimri’s seven-day idolatry evaluation: nature not duration
**Claim:** Zimri could not have practiced much cult in seven days; authors evaluate nature of action (idolater) not length—hence he does not hold the throne.  
**Quote:** “It is, however, not so much the length of time as the nature of the action that is important to the authors. He is an idolater—and so he does not hold on to the throne.”  
**Locus:** §25 add. n. 16:19 (slice ~ll. 401)

**Priority themes covered:**  
- **Schism causes:** Exodus typology (Moses/Pharaoh), heavy yoke/identity, foolish counsel + divine hardening, “all Israel” legitimacy vs de facto Judah, Shemaiah, Adoram/*mas*  
- **Sin of Jeroboam refrain:** characteristic sin → exile; trust failure; persistence (13:33–34); walks-in-sin formulas (Nadab, Baasha, Omri, Ahab)  
- **Golden calves / Exodus echo:** Aaron/Exod 32:4; Deut 4/14:9 idolatry; Bethel house; Asherah/Ahab link  
- **Prophecy-fulfillment:** Ahijah (schism, house doom, reed/exile); man of God/Josiah horizon + short signs; Jehu vs Baasha; Hiel/Jericho; dual causality  
- **Judean evaluation formulas:** Judah did evil; Abijam/Asa patterns; lamp for David; high places limit  
- **Omride / Elijah setup:** Omri–Samaria; Ahab+Jezebel+Baal; delayed judgment → Elijah  

**Out of range / not claimed:** nothing beyond §25; no live wiki pages edited.  

**NEW page flags (sustained):** Jeroboam, Rehoboam, Asa, Ahab; supporting figures Ahijah, Baasha, Omri, Jezebel, man of God / old prophet of Bethel as narrative agents rather than full biography candidates unless integrator decides otherwise.

---

**Claim count:** 45  
**Key theses (Provan):** (1) Division is a second Exodus that collapses into a second golden-calf apostasy. (2) Jeroboam’s sin is politicized, untrusting cultic innovation—the northern refrain unto exile. (3) Prophetic word governs history even when prophets disobey; David’s house is secure by divine choice more than by perfect piety. (4) Judah shares northern-style sin but receives 2 Sam 7 discipline, not extinction oracles. (5) Omride climax multiplies sin and sets the stage for Elijah under the major theme: God’s control of history.
